text: A bullock, a lamb or a pair of doves: God accepted every size of burnt offering. Your capacity to see Jesus is what grows.
explanation:
Leviticus 1 describes three burnt offerings: a bull from the herd for those who could afford it, a sheep or goat, and for the poorest, turtledoves or pigeons. Each one rose as "a sweet aroma to the Lord," because each pictured His Son. God never said, "Come back when you can bring a bull." A woman who only touched the hem of His garment received all the healing she needed.

Yet the sizes speak of capacity. Only for the bull does Scripture mention laying hands on its head, and skinning it and cutting it in pieces. A bigger revelation of Jesus enlarges what you can receive. "Grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord." Whatever size your offering today, keep growing in your view of Him.

text: In Hebrew, Leviticus is called Vayikra, "And He called." The word for offering, korban, means to draw near.
explanation:
Leviticus is the book many believers skip, yet it opens with God calling, not demanding. "Now the Lord called to Moses… 'When any one of you brings an offering to the Lord…'" The Hebrew for offering, korban, comes from a root meaning to come near. Every sacrifice in the book was God's way of bringing people close.

All those offerings point to the one sacrifice of Jesus. Because of Him you don't stand at a distance hoping you're good enough. "Having boldness to enter the Holiest by the blood of Jesus… let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith." The offering has been made. You're called near.

text: The worshipper laid his hand on the bullock's head: his sin went onto it, and its perfection came onto him.
explanation:
"He shall put his hand on the head of the burnt offering, and it will be accepted on his behalf." The word for accepted, ratzah, carries the idea of delight and pleasure. Laying on hands was identification. The spotless animal took the offerer's place and died as if it were guilty, while the offerer was received with all its unblemished acceptance.

That's what happened when you put your faith in Jesus. Your sins went to Him; His righteousness came to you. So stop identifying with what you were: lost, condemned, under the curse. Identify with Him. You're accepted in the Beloved, and God takes delight in you.

text: To create the world, God only had to speak. To forgive you, He had to bleed.
explanation:
When the prodigal came home, his father said, "Bring the fatted calf here and kill it." Animals were usually slaughtered out of sight, behind the house. But this father wanted it done in front of his son, so that he would see what his forgiveness had cost.

The calf wasn't fattened for work in the fields; it was raised for this one day of sacrifice. Jesus came for the same purpose. Your forgiveness is free to you, but it wasn't cheap. And because the price was so great, you never have to wonder whether it was enough.

text: "A sweet aroma to the Lord" is literally an aroma of rest. Every time you draw near, God smells His Son on you.
explanation:
The Hebrew phrase is reach nichoach, an aroma of rest, from the same root as Noah's name. When Noah stepped off the ark and offered burnt offerings, "the Lord smelled a soothing aroma," and He promised never again to curse the ground. God finds His rest in the sacrifice of His Son.

And now "we are to God the fragrance of Christ." When old Isaac blessed Jacob, he said, "The smell of my son is like the smell of a field which the Lord has blessed." Isaac was fooled; God isn't. He sees what Jesus did, and every time you pray, you come wrapped in that fragrance. Picture that, and you'll find yourself coming to Him at every turn.

text: The Hebrew for peace offering is plural, shelamim: peace for spirit, soul and body. And shalom shares its root with paying in full.
explanation:
Shalom already means completeness: health, wholeness, well-being. Leviticus puts it in the plural, peace in all its fullness. The same root gives the Hebrew verb for paying, making whole what was owed. Your peace was paid for, and it cost God His Son: "The chastisement for our peace was upon Him."

Notice too that the fat of the peace offering, the choicest part, was burned on top of the burnt offering already on the altar. Peace rests on the foundation of the burnt offering, our acceptance and righteousness in Christ. Know you're righteous in Him, and wholeness has something to stand on.

text: The Lord restored Job's losses, twice as much, when he prayed for the friends who had wronged him.
explanation:
Job's friends had added to his suffering with wrong words about God. God told them to bring burnt offerings, "and My servant Job shall pray for you." Job took a priest's place for the very people who had hurt him. "And the Lord restored Job's losses when he prayed for his friends. Indeed the Lord gave Job twice as much as he had before."

Under the law, the priest who offered someone's burnt offering kept its skin for himself. When you see those who've spoken against you as the righteousness of God in Christ and bless them, you share in the benefits of that offering. Try it: "Father, thank You that they're righteous in Christ. Give them wisdom and revelation. I bless them."

text: "My people will dwell in a peaceful habitation, in secure dwellings, and in quiet resting places."
explanation:
Isaiah continues, "though hail comes down on the forest, and the city is brought low in humiliation." The storms are real. Forests fall and cities are laid low. But God makes a distinction: "My people" dwell in peace and security in the middle of it.

Don't expect what the world expects. "The path of the just is like the shining sun, that shines ever brighter unto the perfect day." Ever brighter, not dimmer. Your days ahead are days of hope, not because the world is getting easier, but because you're His, and He has given you quietness and security forever.
